newsitem.title: USA: Carolinas on alert as Fran swirls closer.
newsitem.headline: Carolinas on alert as Fran swirls closer.

text.p: Coastal roads from Georgia to North Carolina were jammed on Wednesday as hundreds of thousands of residents headed inland to escape approaching Hurricane Fran and its 115 mph (185 kmh) winds.

The National Hurricane Center predicted the coastline between 300-year-old Charleston, a city pounded seven years ago by deadly Hurricane Hugo, and the resort area of Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, as Fran's most likely target.

But the storm was so large -- hurricane-force winds extended 145 miles (230 km) from its center and tropical storm force winds 290 miles (465 km) -- that coastal areas from northern Florida to Virginia were put on alert.
Thousands of people were evacuated from coastal counties in South Carolina, North Carolina and Georgia, as authorities warned of the likelihood of heavy storm surge and flooding from the storm.
Gale-force winds were expected to begin lashing the coast by midday on Thursday.

Forecasters issued a hurricane warning stretching from Brunswick, Georgia, to the Virginia border, with a hurricane watch extending north to Chincoteague, Virginia. A tropical storm watch was posted from Flagler Beach, Florida, to Brunswick, Georgia.

Bumper-to-bumper traffic streamed out of Charleston, a graceful southern city known for its antebellum plantations and elegant mansions. Residents of the historic district locked shutters over the windows of their brick homes, antique shops and restaurants closed early and gasoline stations had long lines of customers on Wednesday.
"Emergency shelters are up and running, and evacuations should be complete by morning," said Charleston Mayor Joe Riley. "The people of Charleston learned a lot from Hugo."

Hurricane Hugo, ranked as the second costliest hurricane in U.S. history, slammed into Charleston on Sept. 21, 1989, with winds clocked at more than 140 mph (225 kph). Hugo was blamed for 27 deaths, destroyed 17,000 homes and caused more than $7 billion in damage.
South Carolina Gov. David Beasley declared a statewide state of emergency, and issued a mandatory evacuation order affecting beachfront property and other low-lying areas in six counties.
"This storm is incredibly dangerous and must be taken seriously as the life-threatening force that it is," he said.

At 11 p.m. EDT (0300 GMT) Fran was about 335 miles (540 km) southeast of Charleston, the National Hurricane Center said, at latitude 29.1 north and longitude 76.4 west. The storm had winds of 115 mph (185 kph) and was churning northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
"Hurricane Fran is about as large as Hurricane Hugo, and has the potential to become just as strong," said hurricane center forecaster Ed Rappaport.
Georgia Gov. Zell Miller declared a state of emergency in 11 counties along the coast and urged voluntary evacuations. A mandatory evacuation was ordered for residents of vulnerable barrier islands.
"Most people are leaving right now. We're urging people to leave," said Stacey Livingston, a clerk with the town of Kiawah Island, one of the barrier island resorts south of Charleston.
Farther north, emergency management officials worried about the dangerous strength of Fran began evacuating residents of Ocracoke Island, North Carolina, a low-lying resort island late on Wednesday.
Peter Stone, emergency management manager for the tiny island that is part of North Carolina's famed Outer Banks, said the decision was based on the proximity and strength of the storm.
"It was time to get everybody the hell out of here," Stone said.
Ocracoke, a sliver of flood-prone land near Cape Hatteras, has 800 permanent residents and some 2,000 tourists. Three ferries and a two-lane highway are the only ways to get on and off the island.

At Cape Canaveral, about halfway up the Florida coast, NASA rolled the space shuttle Atlantis back to its massive garage as a precaution against storm conditions, delaying its takeoff. Atlantis, already six weeks late, had been due to blast off on Sept. 14 on a mission to pick up U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid from the Russian Mir space station and drop off her replacement, John Blaha.

The potential for flooding was a serious concern, as forecasters warned of tides of 12 to 16 feet (4 to 5.3 meters) above normal near and northeast of where Fran's center makes landfall. Five to 10 inches (12.5-25 cm) of rain also were expected along Fran's path.
